name: Aquamid / polyacrylamide filler

lead: Aquamid is a gel filler of water and cross-linked polyacrylamide that is not meant to be absorbed, so it is classed as a permanent filler. People choose it for lasting facial volume and contour without repeat sessions.

The gel stays in place as a space-filling implant, so the volume is visible on injection and persists. A prospective multicenter study followed 251 patients for five years after facial treatment, and reviews and complication reports are also published. It is discussed in aesthetic-surgery literature much more than in looksmaxxing communities, where permanent fillers come up mainly as cautionary examples.

paras: A clinician injects it in an office visit, and the result is intended to last without top-ups. Regulatory status varies by country.

Papers on permanent fillers describe foreign-body responses with inflammatory nodules, some appearing years after treatment, plus complication reports specific to polyacrylamide. Because the material persists, correcting a problem can require more than waiting for it to fade.

angle.text: Aquamid is a permanent polyacrylamide filler chosen by people who want lasting facial volume rather than repeat sessions. The gel stays in place, so the volume shows on injection and holds. A five-year prospective study of 251 patients exists, and late reactions are documented in the literature.

lead: Aquamid is a brand of injectable polyacrylamide hydrogel (PAAG), a non-biodegradable water-based gel with a cross-linked polyacrylamide network, used for soft-tissue augmentation. Polyacrylamide hydrogels are classed among the permanent or non-resorbable fillers, in contrast with hyaluronic acid fillers, which the body gradually breaks down.[1][1][2]

Published use includes facial soft-tissue augmentation, and a prospective multicenter study followed 251 patients for five years after facial treatment with Aquamid.[3][4] Related polyacrylamide gels have also been studied as bulking agents for stress urinary incontinence in women.[5] The same literature documents adverse reactions, including inflammatory nodules, some appearing years after injection, and complications that have led to published reports on management.[6][7]

Because the material is not designed to be absorbed, authors of review articles describe the treatment as effectively long-term or permanent, with corresponding implications for correcting unwanted results.[6][1] The product is discussed in aesthetic-surgery literature much more than in looksmaxxing communities, where permanent fillers are mentioned mainly in the context of cautionary or irreversible-procedure discussions.
infobox: Facial soft-tissue augmentation; bulking agent in urology research

paras: Polyacrylamide is a highly water-absorbent polymer that forms a soft gel when hydrated, and cross-linking with agents such as N,N-methylenebisacrylamide creates a hydrogel that swells without dissolving.[8] The polymer itself is described as low in toxicity, while its precursor acrylamide is a neurotoxin and carcinogen, and concern in the filler context has centred on possible monomer contamination.[8]

Wikipedia's article on injectable fillers notes that synthetic fillers such as polyacrylamide and poly(methyl methacrylate) rely on particulate scaffolds and induce fibrotic tissue, rather than forming a degradable network.[9] A 2006 histological study evaluated implants of a polyacrylamide filler alongside a hyaluronic acid filler for biocompatibility.[10]

A 2006 plastic-surgery overview describes Aquamid, silicone and ArteFill among permanent fillers and compares them with semipermanent options such as Radiesse, Sculptra and autologous fat.[1] A 2003 pilot study reported early experience with the hydrogel.[3] The five-year multicenter study examined facial soft-tissue augmentation.[4]

Polyacrylamide gels have also been investigated outside aesthetics, for example as a bulking agent in stress urinary incontinence.[5] A registered clinical study (NCT04715802, 240 participants, started 2006) examines options for breast reconstruction timing and method after removal of polyacrylamide hydrogel, reflecting that the gel has been used and later removed in some patients.[11]

A 2003 pilot study described early experience with Aquamid.[3] A 5-year prospective multicenter study of 251 patients assessed safety and aesthetic results after facial soft-tissue augmentation with Aquamid, and is a large prospective multicenter report.[4] An earlier 2003 study placed small test amounts of ten commercially available fillers into the forearm skin of one of the authors and examined excised sites histologically at several time points to compare biocompatibility and persistence.[12]

Other human-tissue data come from histological series: reviews of biopsies of reactions to permanent fillers, including polyacrylamide gels, examine how the material is handled by tissue over time.[6][2] A 2010 article specifically reported complications after polyacrylamide hydrogel injection for soft-tissue augmentation.[7] No randomized controlled trials were identified.

A histology-based review of biopsies from several European surgeons described permanent synthetic fillers as widely non-toxic and non-immunogenic but acting as foreign bodies that elicit a host response aimed at removing the gel. Inflammatory nodules may develop at injection sites, in some products many years later and in others not.[6]

A separate report catalogued complications following polyacrylamide hydrogel injection for soft-tissue augmentation.[7] The histological literature on filler complications also describes the tissue reactions seen with permanent materials, including Aquamid, as they evolve over time.[2] The Wikipedia article on injectable fillers lists general filler risks including bruising, infection, allergic reactions, delayed necrosis and, rarely, blindness from retrograde embolization.[9]
Authors describe the difficulty of correcting problems with non-resorbable fillers as an inherent feature of their permanence, in contrast with fillers that degrade naturally.[1]

In the United States the FDA regulates fillers as medical devices and only a limited number are approved, while in the UK and EEA they need a CE mark covering manufacturing standards rather than proven efficacy.[9] A 2006 review of permanent fillers discussed the FDA status of the products it covered.[1] Status for polyacrylamide products differs by country.
